prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part for optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange tested it from several directions and the core of the case survived. Nobody disputes that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea, that the result is measured and not inferred, or that it has been reproduced and surpassed in independent laboratories, and the chair's own summary records no member arguing that it is premature. The prize criterion as I understand it, a specific discovery or invention and not a body of work, is met by the lattice step: it lets many atoms be interrogated without Doppler, recoil or light-shift limits, which is what made 10^-18 accuracy and stability reachable. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, with Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clock and Ye for taking lattice clocks to record accuracy and the many-body-limited regime, and the citation I propose is deliberately narrow so that it names the lattice clock and not optical timekeeping in general. Five of eight explicit first-round positions land here for reasons that differ in emphasis, which I read as corroboration of the science, but I do not count that as the argument.
statement.case_against: The serious objection remains that the lattice clock rests on laser cooling (1997), the frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012), so a reader can call it an outstanding refinement of precision metrology and not a new discovery. I weigh that as real but secondary, because the lattice idea changes what is possible and is not a combination of the earlier prizes. Two further costs are genuine. A narrow two-name citation leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and ion-clock groups, and I cannot verify from the file the priority sequence between early lattice proposals and the first operating clocks. And the new-messenger case of IceCube is a stronger candidate on discovery character even though its credit is weaker. If the committee decides that discovery of a new observational window must outrank a measured precision advance, that is a legitimate reason to prefer B007, and I would then want the attribution problem solved before voting for it, not after.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether a new observational window (IceCube) should outrank a measured precision advance as a matter of discovery character, and whether any two- or three-name IceCube credit can be defended against the collaboration, AMANDA and Baikal predecessors.
responses.response: I accept that detecting a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos is a discovery in the plainest sense, and my round-1 remark that I would not object to IceCube as a later prize stands. I do not think discovery character is the only axis, though. A prize also has to say who did the original work, and for B007 I cannot defend a Halzen-Karle pair against the collaboration of hundreds and the AMANDA lineage, and adding Yoshida only moves the omission. The lattice clock is an invention with a measured consequence and a pair that maps onto concept and demonstration without an arbitrary cut. I would move to B007 only if the committee can name the specific conceptual and construction contributions that justify two or three names, and so far the file does not show that.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the lattice-clock step stands apart from cooling, the comb and ion control, and what wording keeps the credit specific without excluding Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom and the ion-clock groups.
responses.response: I think the step is separable because the comb is the readout tool and ion control concerns single quantum systems, while the lattice solves a different problem, namely holding thousands of neutral atoms in a regime where the clock transition is unperturbed. On wording, I would resist widening it. A citation of the form 'for the optical lattice clock' with the magic-wavelength lattice named in it keeps the credit specific, and the contributors you list are not excluded from the science, only from the two-name prize, which is the normal cost of a three-person limit. I agree with you that this cost is real and that none of us has verified the priority timeline, so it should be stated openly as the main residual risk and not hidden behind the clean attribution.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the redefinition of the second should not affect timing, but also warns that four first places could reflect a shared instrument-oriented taste in the room rather than merit.
responses.response: I take the second warning to heart. Several of us who work with measurement and instrumentation (I include myself as an electron-microscopy person) are likely to favour a result that is measured and reproducible, and I should discount that. The way I try to do so is to ask whether the claim would stand if a theorist or an astrophysicist were judging it, and I think it does, because the claim is about a specific invention and its measured performance and not about taste. On the redefinition I agree with you: the clocks are already compared at 10^-18 across laboratories, and tying a prize to a metrological decision would be a category error.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers fluctuation theorems (B002) as an exact conceptual discovery about nature and also lists B018 as an alternative, while acknowledging that no colleague corroborated his first place and that Crooks is an awkward omission.
responses.response: The conceptual elegance of fluctuation relations is not in doubt for me, and I respect the argument that exact results far from equilibrium are rare. My difficulty is the criterion of a discovery or invention with identifiable originators. You yourself name three separable steps and four credited names for three places, and the steady-state relation has contested priority, so the prize would have to arbitrate a priority dispute that the file does not resolve. I notice that you place B018 as your own alternative and call its credit clean; if the committee cannot settle B002 on credit, that is a reason to move toward a configuration both of us regard as clean.

responses.point: Johansson prefers Cirac and Zoller (B032) as a theoretical idea that defined an experimental field, and is open to B018 if breadth of conviction counts.
responses.response: I do not want breadth of conviction to substitute for scientific judgment either, and I do not rest on it. On the science, I find the Cirac-Zoller proposals original and mature, and I agree with your point that the 2012 prize recognised the experimental side and not the proposals. My remaining concern is the one you raised yourself: a prize on B032 affects B015, and a theory-only prize in a field whose experimental half is only partly recognised invites a coherence question the three-person limit makes hard to answer. I would not oppose B032 as a later prize, but I keep it behind the lattice clock for now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice step as sufficiently distinct from the earlier cooling, frequency-comb and ion-control prizes; I judge it distinct but the question is a matter of weight.
The priority sequence between early lattice proposals and the first operating lattice clocks, and the roles of Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and others, rests on recollection and is unverified.
Whether the committee will rank discovery of a new messenger above a measured precision advance, which would favour B007 if its attribution can be settled.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing, which I think it should not.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. I record again my long-running academic exchange with Japanese universities, including a University of Tokyo fellowship, and that Katori is based in Japan; this is institutional proximity, not a collaboration, and I do not think it requires recusal. Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson is on the committee but has no apparent link to B018. I have no documented tie to Halzen, Karle, Yoshida, Cirac, Zoller, Moodera, Miyazaki or Parkin, and I should discount my own preference for measurement-driven, instrument-based results as a bias.
